title: Tanzania Ground Handler Contracts: What to Settle Before Your First Client Lands
meta_title: Tanzania Ground Handler Questions for Tour Operators
meta_description: What to ask a Tanzania ground handler before you sign: licences, vehicles, park fees, the new entry insurance, deposits and emergency cover.
excerpt: A practical guide for tour operators and travel agents choosing a Tanzania ground handler: licences, vehicles, park fees, entry insurance and contract terms to settle first.
content:
A Tanzania ground handler is the licensed local company that turns your client's itinerary into vehicles, guides, park permits and lodge bookings on the ground. Before you contract one, confirm its tourism licence, who owns the safari vehicles, how park fees and the new entry insurance are paid, and who answers the phone at night.

Choosing badly is expensive: vehicles turn out to be hired in, fees were priced on last year's tariff, or nobody planned the handover from a Kenya leg. This guide sets out the questions we would ask a Tanzania ground handler if we were in your seat, with the paperwork to request and the answers that should make you pause. Our safari DMC service for travel agents and tour leaders works to the same standard when we plan Tanzania programmes from Nairobi.

Quick Facts

  • Who licenses tour companies: The Tourism Division of Tanzania's Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism, under the Tourism Act
  • Industry body: Tanzania Association of Tour Operators (TATO), based in Arusha; membership is voluntary
  • Vehicles: Tanzanian-registered safari vehicles only inside Tanzania's parks; Kenyan-plated vehicles stop at the border
  • Entry insurance: Mandatory for visitors since 1 October 2026: US$44 adults, US$22 children 3-17, infants free (checked November 2026)
  • Main hub: Arusha, about 5 to 6 hours by road from Nairobi via the Namanga border
  • Key parks: Serengeti, Tarangire and Lake Manyara (TANAPA) and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area (separate authority)

What Does a Tanzania Ground Handler Actually Do?

A Tanzania ground handler delivers everything your client experiences once they land: airport meet and greet, safari vehicles and driver-guides, lodge and camp bookings, park and conservation fees, internal flights, and support if something goes wrong. You sell the trip and hold the client relationship; the handler runs it on the ground.

In northern Tanzania most handlers are based in Arusha, close to Kilimanjaro International Airport and the start of the classic circuit through Tarangire, Lake Manyara, the Serengeti and the Ngorongoro Crater. Some own a large fleet and employ their guides; others hire vehicles and freelance guides as bookings come in. Both can work, but know which kind of Tanzania ground handler you are buying, because it decides how much control it has on a busy August day.

Ground handler, DMC or local tour operator?

The terms overlap. A destination management company usually covers more than safaris (conferences, incentives, several countries), while a ground handler focuses on running trips you have sold. What matters is what the company contracts to deliver, and who is responsible when a supplier lets your client down. Our guide to what an East Africa DMC does for overseas agents explains the wider role.

Which Licences Should a Tanzania Ground Handler Show You?

A Tanzania ground handler should show you a current tourism licence issued by the Tourism Division of the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism, which registers and licenses tourism businesses under the Tourism Act. Mountain climbing and tour operation are licensed as separate activities, so check the licence covers what you are buying.

Ask for the licence certificate itself, not a logo on a website, then check that the company name, licence category and validity dates match the business that will invoice you. If the invoice comes from a different company than the one on the licence, ask why before you go further. Tanzania cut several tourism licence fees in its 2025/26 budget and now requires those payments in Tanzanian shillings, so a well-run company will have up-to-date paperwork without fuss.

Licence checks for a Tanzania ground handler

  • A tourism licence in the company's own name, valid for your travel dates
  • A separate mountain climbing licence if the handler will run Kilimanjaro or Mount Meru climbs
  • Business registration and tax identification documents that match the invoicing company
  • Public liability insurance details, and the insurer's name
  • Membership of the Tanzania Association of Tour Operators, if claimed, confirmed with the association

TATO membership is voluntary and is not a licence, but it shows a company takes part in the industry's own standards. In May 2025 TATO launched a code of conduct for driver-guides covering wildlife protection, vehicle safety, guest welfare and cultural respect, starting with training for 530 guides in Arusha. Ask whether the guides you will get have been through it.

Who Owns the Vehicles, and Why Kenyan Plates Stop at the Border

Ask every Tanzania ground handler whether the safari vehicles are its own or hired in, and get the answer in writing. Owned vehicles usually mean better maintenance and faster replacement after a breakdown, while a handler that hires in at peak season may struggle to find enough good vehicles for a large group.

Tanzania's parks only accept Tanzanian-registered safari vehicles. Kenyan-plated vehicles cannot operate inside the Serengeti or Ngorongoro, so on a combined trip with the Masai Mara your clients change vehicle, normally at the Namanga border (about 5 to 6 hours from Nairobi to Arusha by road including the border) or by taking a regional flight. A good Tanzania ground handler times the swap so nobody waits in the heat at the border post. Our post on combining Kenya and Tanzania on one safari shows how the routing works.

What to askA good answerA warning sign
How many vehicles do you own?A clear number, with photos and registration details"We always find vehicles"
Seats per vehicle for my groupWindow seats guaranteed, usually six or seven clients per vehicleEight or nine to a vehicle to save cost
Pop-up roof and chargingEvery vehicle has a pop-up roof, USB charging and a cool box"Most of our vehicles have them"
Breakdown planA named replacement vehicle within a set number of hoursNo plan until it happens

Driver-guides

Ask for guide names as soon as a group confirms, along with their languages, years of experience in the parks on your itinerary and first aid training. For groups with several vehicles, ask who the lead guide is and whether each guide stays with the same clients for the whole trip.

How Are Park Fees, Taxes and the New Entry Insurance Handled?

Most Tanzania ground handlers pay national park and Ngorongoro fees on your clients' behalf and pass them through in the net rate. Ask for those fees as a separate line per person per day, with VAT shown clearly, so you can see exactly what is a government charge and what is the handler's service.

The Serengeti, Tarangire and Lake Manyara are run by Tanzania National Parks, and fees are set and published on the Tanzania National Parks (TANAPA) website, while the Ngorongoro Crater sits under its own conservation authority with separate entry and crater service fees. Fees change from time to time, so your contract should say what happens if a tariff rises after you have confirmed a booking. Our post on Tanzania park fees for the Serengeti, Ngorongoro, Tarangire and Manyara sets out the current fees.

The mandatory inbound travel insurance

Since 1 October 2026 every foreign visitor needs Tanzania's government inbound travel insurance, bought before arrival through the official portal for the first point of entry: mainland Tanzania or Zanzibar. One policy covers a combined itinerary. It costs US$44 per adult and US$22 per child aged 3 to 17, infants travel free, and groups of 10 or more adults get 10% off (checked November 2026, as reported by the African Travel and Tourism Association).

The policy lasts up to 92 days and covers emergency medical treatment, evacuation, repatriation and lost luggage, but it does not replace your clients' own travel insurance. Agree with your Tanzania ground handler who buys it, who checks every certificate before departure and what happens if a client arrives without one. Visas are separate again; our Tanzania visa guide covers the eVisa.

Cost itemWho usually pays itWhat to confirm
National park feesThe handler, passed through at costPer person per day, VAT shown, rule for fee changes
Ngorongoro entry and crater feesThe handlerWhether the crater service fee is per vehicle or per person
Inbound travel insuranceThe client or agent, before arrivalWho buys it and who checks each certificate
Lodges and campsThe handler, under its own contractsDeposit dates and the lodge's own cancellation terms

Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar: Services That Are Often Subcontracted

Kilimanjaro climbs and Zanzibar beach stays are the two parts of a Tanzania trip most often passed to another company. That is not wrong in itself, but your Tanzania ground handler should tell you upfront who actually runs each part and who is responsible to you if it goes badly.

Kilimanjaro climbs

For a climb, ask for the mountain climbing licence, the guide-to-client ratio, how oxygen and pulse oximeters are carried, the evacuation plan from each camp, and how porters are paid, fed, equipped and kept to safe loads. In August 2026 the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism reminded the industry that only the government decides whether a mountain company is legally allowed to operate, and that private porter-welfare programmes are voluntary. Membership of such a programme is still a good sign, but the licence comes first. For group climbs, our post on planning a Kilimanjaro group climb goes into route choice and pacing.

Zanzibar extensions

Zanzibar has its own tourism licensing and its own insurance portal. If your Tanzania ground handler books the beach part through a Zanzibar partner, ask for that partner's name, who meets your clients at the airport and who they call if a transfer goes wrong.

What Should Your Contract With a Tanzania Ground Handler Cover?

A contract with a Tanzania ground handler should cover what is included, payment and deposit dates, cancellation terms that follow the lodges' own rules, how fee or tax changes are passed on, emergency procedures and response times, and who is liable when a subcontractor fails. Short, clear clauses beat a long document nobody reads.

Deposits deserve the closest look. A fair Tanzania ground handler asks for deposits that match its real outlays, such as camp deposits and early flight bookings, rather than a large blanket sum months ahead. Ask for a payment schedule tied to the lodges' own deadlines, and pay into a company account in the licensed company's name. For our own partner terms, see the Kenya and Tanzania B2B agent rates page.

  • Inclusions and exclusions: listed per service, including drinks, tips, laundry and the inbound insurance
  • Price changes: government fees and taxes passed on at cost, with proof; no other changes after confirmation
  • Cancellations: tied to each lodge's terms, so you are never charged more than the handler loses
  • Emergencies: a 24-hour number, a named manager and evacuation cover such as the Flying Doctors emergency evacuation membership
  • Complaints: how a problem is reported during the trip and how quickly it is fixed

How to Test a New Partner Before You Send a Big Group

The safest way to test a new Tanzania ground handler is to start small: send a couple or a family of four on a classic northern circuit before you trust the company with a 30-person incentive. You learn more from one real trip than from any presentation.

Send a realistic brief and watch the reply. A strong Tanzania ground handler comes back within a day or two with a programme that fits the season, asks sensible questions about your clients and flags problems, such as a Ngorongoro night that is hard to get in July. A weak one sends a standard itinerary with your clients' name pasted in. For something closer to a finished product, our 8 day midrange Tanzania safari shows the level of detail we put into a lodge-based programme, and the Tanzania safari packages page shows the full range.

If your clients combine countries, ask whether one partner can run both sides. One contract for a Kenya and Tanzania trip saves you two payment schedules and an awkward handover between companies, as long as the Tanzanian side still runs on Tanzanian vehicles and licensed guides. Our checklist for choosing a Kenya safari DMC covers the Kenyan side of the same question, and the group safaris section shows the kinds of groups we plan for.

Insider Tips

  • Check the licence yourself: Ask for the certificate and confirm the company name matches your invoices
  • Get vehicles in writing: Number, seats per vehicle and window seats for every client
  • Ask for a fee line: Park and Ngorongoro fees shown separately, with VAT
  • Settle the insurance: Agree who buys Tanzania's inbound policy and who checks it
  • Name the subcontractors: Kilimanjaro, Zanzibar and flights, with who is responsible to you
  • Start with a small booking: Test the handler on two to four clients before a large group

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a Tanzania ground handler need a licence?

Yes. A Tanzania ground handler that sells or runs tours must be licensed by the Tourism Division of the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism under the Tourism Act. Ask for the licence certificate, check that the company name and licence category match the services you are buying, and confirm it is current for the dates your clients travel.

Can a Kenyan safari vehicle drive into the Serengeti?

No. Kenyan-registered safari vehicles cannot operate inside Tanzania's national parks, so a Kenya and Tanzania combination needs a change of vehicle, usually at the Namanga border or in Arusha, or a regional flight. Your Tanzania ground handler should name the Tanzanian vehicles and guides that take over and show how the handover is timed.

Who buys Tanzania's mandatory inbound travel insurance?

Each visitor needs the government inbound travel insurance, introduced on 1 October 2026, bought through the official portal for their first point of entry: mainland Tanzania or Zanzibar. It costs US$44 for adults and US$22 for children aged 3 to 17 (checked November 2026). Agree in writing whether you, your client or the ground handler buys it.

Should Tanzania park fees be included in a ground handler's net rate?

Usually yes. Most agents ask a Tanzania ground handler to include national park and Ngorongoro fees in the net rate, listed as a separate line, because the handler pays them on entry. Ask the handler to show fees per person per day, state whether VAT is included and explain what happens to your price if the authorities change fees after you confirm.

How do I test a new Tanzania ground handler?

The safest way to test a new Tanzania ground handler is with a small, simple booking before a large group: two or four travellers on a classic northern circuit. Watch how fast they answer, how clear the documents are and how they handle a small change. A short inspection trip with their guide also tells you a lot.

Final Thoughts

The right Tanzania ground handler is the one that can prove its licence, shows you the vehicles and guides it will send, prices fees and insurance clearly and answers at three in the morning. Ask those questions before you sign, start with a small group, and you protect both your clients and your own name.
